item.title: Software Engineering at Google, Ch 14: Larger Testing
item.description: How did a Google test end up as an internet mystery on YouTube? In this deep dive on Chapter 14 of Software Engineering at Google (Winters, Manshreck & Wright; chapter by Joseph Graves), we explore larger tests: why fidelity is the reason they exist, the gaps unit tests leave (unfaithful doubles, configuration, load, unanticipated behavior, and the "vacuum effect"), why larger tests are slow, flaky, and hard to own, the anatomy of a system under test, record/replay, test data and verification, and a tour of Google's larger tests, from A/B diffs and probers to DiRT disaster drills and chaos engineering, plus how to keep them fast, understandable, and owned. item.title: Software Engineering at Google, Ch 13: Test Doubles
item.description: Why did Google's love affair with mocking frameworks turn into a maintenance bill? In this deep dive on Chapter 13 of Software Engineering at Google (Winters, Manshreck & Wright; chapter by Andrew Trenk and Dillon Bly), we unpack test doubles: seams and dependency injection, the three techniques of faking, stubbing, and interaction testing, why Google prefers real implementations and classical over mockist testing, the @DoNotMock annotation, how to judge fidelity and when to write a fake, the dangers of overusing stubs, change-detector tests, and why state testing beats interaction testing. item.title: Software Engineering at Google, Ch 12: Unit Testing
item.description: Why can a screen full of failing tests contain zero real bugs? In this deep dive on Chapter 12 of Software Engineering at Google (Winters, Manshreck & Wright; chapter by Erik Kuefler), we unpack Google's case that unit-test quality is a maintainability problem: brittle versus unchanging tests, the four kinds of code change, testing through public APIs, state over interactions, complete and concise tests, testing behaviors instead of methods, given/when/then structure, behavior-based names, no logic in tests, clear failure messages, and why test code should be DAMP rather than DRY. item.title: Software Engineering at Google, Ch 11: Testing Overview
item.description: Why did Google stop trusting smart engineers alone to keep bugs out? In this deep dive on Chapter 11 of Software Engineering at Google (Winters, Manshreck & Wright; chapter by Adam Bender), we follow the Google Web Server's turnaround from a mostly-rolled-back release process to a test-every-change culture, then unpack the chapter's toolkit: test size versus scope, hermetic and flaky tests, the 80/15/5 test pyramid and its ice-cream-cone and hourglass antipatterns, the Beyoncé Rule, why code coverage misleads, and how bathroom flyers and a five-level certification ladder changed engineering habits without a leadership mandate.
